25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Priests keep watch in three places in the Temple out of honor for the Temple.
Names the chambers of Avtinas, the Spark and the Hearth as watch posts, including their two-sided placement.
Chambers of Avtinas and the Spark have upper stories where young priests keep watch.
The Hearth chamber has no upper story; its ceiling is cupola-shaped and it is a large hall.
The hall is surrounded by rows of stone that serve as benches.
Elders of the patrilineal family sleep there and hold the Temple courtyard keys.
Young priests sleep on the floor with their garments, not on the benches.
They do not sleep in the sacred vestments.
They remove and fold the vestments and place them under their heads.
They cover themselves with their own non-sacred garments.
Case: a priest suffers a seminal emission and becomes unfit for service.
That priest leaves the Hearth chamber and walks away.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The priest walks under the arch with lamps lit on both sides until reaching the Chamber of Immersion, where a fire burns.
A bathroom of honor exists; a closed door tells the next user that someone is inside.
An open door signals that no one is inside, so one may enter.
The priest descends, immerses, ascends, dries off and warms himself.
He warms himself opposite the fire, then returns to sit with his fellow priests.
He waits in the Hearth chamber until dawn, when the gates open, then leaves.
Whoever wants to remove the ashes from the altar rises early and immerses before the appointed priest arrives.
At what time does the appointed priest arrive?
His arrival times vary; he may come at the rooster's call or shortly before or after it.
The appointed priest arrives, knocks, and the priests inside open the gate for him.
He announces that whoever has immersed may come forward to take part in the lottery.
They conduct the lottery, and whoever wins the lot gains the right to the task.
From where is this rule derived?
Abaye says it is derived from a verse.
Numbers 3:38 is quoted, describing Moses, Aaron and his sons keeping the Sanctuary watch.
The verse shows that a watch in general is required of priests and Levites.
The Mishna teaches separate watch places for priests and Levites, but the verse writes them together.
The verse is read as Moses keeping watch in one place, Aaron in one place, and his sons in two others.
How do we know the verse should be read this way, with separate watches written separately?
Perhaps all the priests watch in one shared separate place, but that cannot be, since Moses's place is singular.
Rav Ashi says the halakha is derived from the end of the verse.
Numbers 3:38 is quoted again, using three forms of the root for watch, indicating three separate watches.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna names the Chamber of Avtinas and the Chamber of the Spark.
Were these chambers actual upper stories, or merely tall halls built on pillars that resembled upper stories?
A mishna about the Gate of the Spark describes an upper story where priests watched from above and Levites from below.
From where is it derived that priests and Levites kept watch on different stories?
Numbers 18:2 is cited, stating that the Levites accompany Aaron in his service.
Does the verse refer to the priests' watch or to the Levites' own service of bearing vessels?
Numbers 18:4 is cited, saying the Levites keep watch over the vessels and the service.
The watch-keeping in Numbers 18:4 already covers their own service, so the earlier verse must refer to the priests' watch.
How then is the earlier verse to be understood, and how exactly?
Priests keep watch from above and Levites accompany them from below.
The Chamber of the Hearth had a cupola-shaped ceiling and was a large hall.
Was there only one watchman stationed in the Chamber of the Hearth?
A mishna says the Chamber of the Hearth had two gates, one opening to the rampart and one to the courtyard, implying two watchmen.
Rabbi Yehuda explains that the courtyard gate had a small wicket through which priests could look into the courtyard.
Abaye says the two gates stood opposite each other, so one watchman could oversee both.
The Chamber of the Hearth was surrounded by rows of stone serving as benches.
What exactly were these rows of stone?
They were chiseled stones forming steps by which priests climbed to another row to lie down.
Would the stones have been split during construction, given the prohibition on iron tools in building the Temple?
1 Kings 6:7 is cited, stating no iron tool was heard while the Temple was built.
Abaye says the stones were cut outside the Temple area and brought in from the start, small and large.
1 Kings 7:10 is cited, describing stones of ten and eight cubits used in the foundation.
The elders of the patrilineal family serving the next day would sleep there on the rows of stone.
Why did they sleep on the stones instead of bringing beds into the chamber?
Abaye says bringing beds into the Temple is not proper conduct.
The young priests each slept with his garment on the ground.
Why does the mishna call the younger priests here by one term and call them rovim in the earlier passage?

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the question of why the young priests are called pirhei kehuna here but rovim there.
Priests not yet eligible for service are called rovim; those ready to serve in the Hearth chamber are called pirhei kehuna.
Middot 1:1 is cited: priests keep watch in three places, Avtinas, the Spark and the Hearth.
Levites keep watch in twenty-one places around the Temple Mount and courtyard, plus three inner chambers.
From where are these Levite watch places derived?
Rav Yehuda of Sura, or a baraita, teaches the derivation from Chronicles.
1 Chronicles 26:17-18 is cited, listing the Levite gatekeepers and their watch posts.
The Sages object that the listed watches total twenty-four, not twenty-one, so this cannot be the source.
Abaye says the verse repeats two for the Asuppim, which always have only two watchmen.
Even so, twenty-two watches remain; the Parbar watch had one guard, and the second Levite only accompanied him.
What is the meaning of the term laParbar in the verse?
Rabba bar Rav Sheila says it contracts two Aramaic words meaning toward the outside.
Alternatively, there are twenty-four watches in all: three of the priests and twenty-one of the Levites.
But the verse writes that all twenty-four watches are kept by Levites.
This follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who holds that priests are sometimes called Levites in the Bible.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says twenty-four places in Scripture call priests Levites, and this verse is one.
Ezekiel 44:15 is cited, calling the sons of Zadok the priests the Levites.
Mishna: five watches at the Temple Mount gates, four at its corners within the wall; five at courtyard gates, four outside its wall.
What distinguishes the Temple Mount watches kept inside the wall from the courtyard watches kept outside it?
Sitting is allowed on the Temple Mount but not in the courtyard, so watches there are placed where the watchman may sit.
But was it only five gates that were built into the courtyard walls?
A mishna says there were seven courtyard gates: three north, three south, and one east.
Abaye says two of the gates, leading to the Spark and Hearth chambers, needed no Levite watch since priests kept watch there.
Rava says the number of gates is a dispute among tanna'im, as a baraita teaches.
The baraita: no fewer than thirteen treasurers and seven trustees; Rabbi Natan says thirteen treasurers for thirteen gates.
Removing the five Mount gates leaves eight courtyard gates, so tanna'im disagree on whether there were eight, seven or five.
The mishna teaches that priests did not sleep dressed in sacred vestments.
The Gemara infers that only sleeping is forbidden in the vestments, so walking in them is permitted and they may be used.
The Sages reject that inference: walking in the vestments is also not permitted.
The mishna mentions sleeping only because it wishes to teach the clause about folding and placing the vestments, so the opening clause is also about sleeping.
The mishna's words about placing vestments under the head would then suggest benefit from them, so the Gemara reads it as beside the head.
Rav Pappa infers from this reading that phylacteries may be placed beside the head during sleep.
Beside the head is the reasonable reading, since beneath the head would violate the prohibition on mixed wool and linen.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: On one view the High Priest's belt differs from an ordinary priest's belt, which is all linen.
On the other view the ordinary priest's belt is the same as the High Priest's, so it contains mixed kinds.
If so, what can be said to resolve the difficulty?
Perhaps mixed kinds are prohibited only when worn or placed on oneself, but spreading them beneath is permitted.
A baraita forbids spreading mixed kinds beneath oneself, lest a fiber wrap around the flesh.
Even with a separating layer it is forbidden, as shown by a baraita about ten mattresses over a mixed garment.
The mishna must therefore permit the vestments only beside the head, not beneath it.
Alternatively, the mishna refers to vestments that contain no mixed kinds.
Rav Ashi says priestly vestments, especially the belt, are stiff, so lying on them is permitted.
Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, is cited: stiff felt from Neresh is permitted because it gives no warmth and is not a garment.
A baraita permits wearing priestly vestments within the Temple but not leaving to the country; so benefit from them is permitted.
Is it not permitted to wear the vestments in the rest of the country outside the Temple?
A baraita about Gerizim and Shimon HaTzaddik shows him wearing priestly vestments outside the Temple.
Either he wore garments fit to be priestly vestments, or he wore consecrated ones, permitted due to the need of the hour.
Psalms 119:126 is cited to justify violating the halakha for the sake of Heaven in times of great need.
Mishna: a priest with a seminal emission leaves the Chamber of the Hearth and goes through the passage beneath the Temple.
This mishna supports Rabbi Yohanan, who holds the tunnels were not sanctified and an impure man is sent outside two camps.
Mishna: lamps burn on both sides of the passage, and there is a bathroom of honor in the Chamber of Immersion.
Rav Safra sits in the bathroom when Rabbi Abba arrives and coughs; Rav Safra tells him to enter.
Rabbi Abba rebukes Rav Safra for behaving like a man of Seir, the land of the Edomites, by letting him enter.
The mishna teaches that a closed door means someone is inside, so one must wait for him to leave.
Does this mean one should not have entered at all?
Rav Safra feared Rabbi Abba might be in danger, since holding back feces or urine causes illness, as a baraita teaches.
Rav and Rav Huna each instruct their sons on relieving themselves in the dark or before dawn.
Relieve yourself when the streets are empty, and behave modestly: sit before uncovering and cover before standing.
When drinking water, pour out a little to rinse the cup before passing it to a student.
A baraita forbids giving the remainder of one's water to a student without first pouring some out; a student died of thirst after refusing it.
The Sages rule that one must not give water to a student without first pouring some out.
Rav Ashi says a student who pours out in his teacher's presence is not guilty of disrespect.
Rules on spitting in a teacher's presence: do not do so, except when eating gourd or porridge, which is dangerous to hold back.
Mishna: the Temple Mount officer goes around each watch post with torches to ensure the watchmen are awake.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: the watchman is greeted; silence shows he is asleep, and the Temple Mount officer may strike him and burn his garment.
Bystanders hear the noise and explain that a Levite is being beaten and his clothing burned for sleeping on watch.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov reports that his maternal uncle was found sleeping on watch and his garment was burned.
Rabbi Yohanan praises early generations who judged even unavoidable sleep, and all the more so deliberate offenses.
A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: love admonition, because where the wise rebuke, blessing and goodness enter the world.
Proverbs 24:25 is cited: to those who admonish there shall be delight and a good blessing.
Another view holds that one should hold fast to exceptional faithfulness in dealings.
Psalms 101:6 is cited: my eyes are upon the faithful of the land.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani, citing Rabbi Yonatan, says one who rebukes for Heaven's sake merits a portion with God.
Proverbs 28:23 is cited: one who rebukes a man shall find favor.
Such a rebuker is also drawn under a cord of divine kindness.
Proverbs 28:23 is cited again: he who rebukes finds more favor than one who flatters with the tongue.
Mishna quoted: one who finds the bathroom door closed waits, and whoever wants to remove the ashes rises early to immerse.
The mishna seems to contradict itself: it implies the ash removal is decided by readiness, yet later by a lottery.
Abaye: the first clause describes the procedure before the lottery ordinance, the second clause after it.
An earlier mishna is cited: originally whoever wished removed the ashes, with a race to the altar ramp and a finger lottery for ties.
Explanation of the finger lottery: one or two fingers may be shown, but never the thumb, which could enable manipulation.
Two priests raced and one shoved the other, breaking his leg; the court then instituted that ash removal be done only by lottery.
Rava: both clauses describe the procedure after the ordinance, and the mishna teaches that those who wish to participate rise early.
Rava's reading: whoever wants to participate in the lottery rises early and immerses before the appointed priest arrives.
Mishna: the appointed priest opens the wicket from the Chamber of the Hearth, and the priests enter with two torches.
The priests split into two groups, walking the portico from east and from west, inspecting the vessels.
They inspect each vessel until they reach the chamber of the preparer of the griddle-cake offering.
Both groups declare that all is well and the vessels are in place, and they set the preparer to his task.
The priest who won the lottery removes the ashes, while the others remind him of the requirements.
Reminder not to touch any vessel until hands and feet are sanctified from the Basin.
The coal pan is placed in the corner between the ramp and the altar, on the western side of the ramp.
No one enters with the ash-removing priest, and he walks by the light of the altar's fire unseen by others.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Priests could not hear the offerer; they knew he had purified hands and feet from the sound of the basin pulleys.
The offerer takes the coal pan, ascends the altar, clears the coals and descends the ramp.
He walks to the floor, turns north and deposits the coals at a set spot near the ramp.
Were there porticoes in the Temple courtyard at all?
A baraita is brought against the view that porticoes existed, naming R. Eliezer ben Yaakov as its source.
The baraita cites a verse forbidding a tree beside the altar as its proof.
The verse is explained as forbidding both idolatrous trees and any wood placed beside the altar.
Rav Hisda upholds the mishna by limiting the prohibition to wooden porticoes, while stone ones are allowed.
The mishna states that the inspectors kept checking the vessels until reaching the griddle-cake preparer's chamber.
Does this mean the griddle-cake offering was brought before the other rites of the service?
A baraita teaches that nothing may be offered on the altar before the morning daily offering.
The baraita supports this with a verse about the burnt offering placed in order before the peace offerings.
Rabba answers that the verse means the burnt offering comes first, so the griddle cakes follow it.
Rav Yehuda explains that the griddle cakes were not burned early, but used to heat water for the cakes.
The Gemara closes the chapter, marking the end of the section on the three places.
Mishnah: the brothers of the ash-remover hurry to purify themselves and climb with shovels and forks.
Unconsumed limbs and fats from the night are cleared to the altar sides, or stacked on the ramp.
The ashes are heaped in the altar's center, removed outside the city, but not on festivals.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The priest who removed the ashes was never lazy about clearing them from the altar.
Priests began raising logs onto the altar to build the wood arrangement for the offerings.
Are all types of wood fit for the arrangement?
Yes, all wood is fit except the vine and the olive tree.
In practice they used branches of fig, nut and pine wood for the arrangement.
The large arrangement was built on the altar's east side, with gaps for kindling to spread the fire.
From the available logs they selected fine fig wood, then built the second arrangement for incense.
The incense arrangement was placed near the southwest corner, four cubits north of it.
It held enough wood for five se'a of coals, eight on Shabbat, and leftover limbs returned to the large pile.
Rava holds that the mishna's ash-heap and gold-cup descriptions are exaggerations, not literal facts.
R. Ami says the Torah, the prophets and the Sages all sometimes used exaggerated language.
He cites the verse describing cities fortified up to heaven as an example of exaggeration in the Torah.
Objection: the cities cannot literally have been fortified up to heaven.
Reply: this is exaggeration, as the Sages also spoke in such figurative language.
Recalls the earlier examples of the ash heap and the gold cup as Sages' exaggerations.
The prophets too used exaggerated language, as the Sages stated.
Cites Solomon's coronation verse, where the earth splitting from the pipe sound is an exaggeration.
Shmuel says the Sages used exaggeration in three cases: the ash heap, the vine, and the Curtain.
Shmuel's teaching excludes Rava's view, citing the mishna that the lamb was given water in a gold cup.
Rava says the gold cup description is an exaggeration.
Shmuel replies that the golden cup was literal, since the Temple is a place of wealth without poverty.
The ash heap is the first of the three cases that Shmuel lists as exaggerations.
A baraita describes the gold vine at the Sanctuary entrance, supporting the vine as the second case.
The vine hung on posts, and each donor could add a gold leaf to it.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A cluster of grapes was hung on the vine; R. Elazar recounts an incident of three hundred priests moving it.
The Gemara cites a mishna describing the Curtain, as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel relates in Rabbi Shimon's name.
The mishna describes the Curtain's thickness, strands, dimensions, cost, and the priests who immersed it each year.
The mishna teaches that wood from olive and vine trees is excluded from the arrangement of wood.
What is the reason that olive and vine wood is unfit?
Rav Pappa says the knots in these branches make the wood burn poorly and smoke excessively.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov adds that using these trees would harm the settlement of Eretz Yisrael.
An objection is raised from a baraita on the Leviticus verse about wood for the altar fire.
The verse requires wood that burns completely, meaning smooth branches without internal knots.
Are all trees' wood fit for the arrangement?
Yes, all wood is fit except olive and vine; priests used fig, nut and pine branches.
The priests customarily used young branches of fig, nut, and pine wood for the arrangement.
R. Eliezer adds that hackberry, oak, palm, carob and sycamore wood are also unfit.
Explains the disagreement: Eliezer and the first tanna differ over wood knotted on the outside.
If olive and vine are excluded for the land's sake, the palm should be excluded too, since it is praised.
Rav Aha replies that the mishna speaks of fig trees that bear no fruit, and so with the palm.
Is there really a fig tree that does not bear fruit?
Yes, growers graft white figs, an inferior variety, which is how fruitless fig trees arise.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Growers plant the tree on a sea-deposit spot; its wood is strong and heavy but bears no fruit.
The mishna says the priest assembled the large wood arrangement, with its opening on the eastern side.
What is the reason the arrangement had an opening?
Rav Huna and Rav Hisda differ: to let wind fan the flames, or to light kindling from there.
An objection from the mishna: kindling was lit from the gap, so the opening was not used for the wind.
Reply: the opening served lighting, and the priests also built many spaces inside the arrangement.
The chapter closes and the next mishna begins, opening with the brothers of the priest who removed ashes.
The overseer invites the priests to draw lots for slaughtering, sprinkling and the altar and Candelabrum ashes.
The mishna lists the limbs and offerings distributed among the priests who carry them up to the altar.
The lottery is drawn, and the priest who wins it gains the right to slaughter the offering.
The overseer asks observers whether daylight has come; Matya ben Shmuel gives a different wording.
The overseer sends for a lamb from the Chamber of the Lambs and describes the four chambers there.
The priests take out silver and gold service vessels and give the daily lamb water in a cup.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The lamb, already examined at dusk, is checked again by torchlight before slaughter.
Mishna: the priests who clear the ashes carry four vessels, including the basket, jug and two keys.
Mishna: the priest comes to the northern wicket of the gate, while the southern one stays closed.
The southern wicket is fixed as closed, and no one enters through it.
The closed wicket is supported by Ezekiel's verse that the gate shall stay shut because God entered through it.
The priest opens the wicket and the large gate, and the slaughterer waits until he hears it open.
Mishna: from Jericho people could hear the gate opening, the shovel instrument, the Levites' song and other sounds.
Some say that from Jericho one could even hear the High Priest pronouncing God's name on Yom Kippur.
From Jericho people could also smell the incense being prepared in the Temple.
Rabbi Elazar ben Diglai's goats near Mikhvar sneezed from the incense smell, supporting the claim about scent carrying.
Mishna: the priest who won the lottery takes the lamb to the slaughterhouse with its hooks and marble tables.
Mishna: the priest who clears ashes from the inner altar gathers them into a basket and carries it out.
Mishna: the priest clearing the Candelabrum checks the lamps, relights them, and removes the ashes.
A three-stepped stone stands before the Candelabrum, and the ashes from both clearings are poured by the altar.
The chapter closes and the overseer addresses the priests to begin the next mishna on binding the lamb.
Mishna: the lamb is tied by pairing each hind leg with its foreleg, with its head to the south and face to the west.
Mishna: twenty-four rings are set north of the altar, and the morning and afternoon lambs are slaughtered at specific corners.
Mishna: the priest sprinkles the blood on the altar corners, then pours the remainder at the southern base.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The priest does not break the hind leg when flaying; he punctures it at the knee and hangs the lamb on hooks.
He flays from the top down, gives the head and the lower legs to the priests, and drains the heart's blood.
He removes the forelegs and the right hind leg for the priests, then opens the midsection to expose the innards.
He places the fats on the head, and the innards are rinsed, the stomach in the courtyard and the rest on the tables.
He separates the lung, lobe and liver, leaves them attached to their places, and gives the breast to a priest.
He cuts the right flank, leaving the spine and two narrow ribs attached, and gives it to a priest.
He gives the cud to a priest, with the windpipe, heart and lung still hanging from it.
He cuts the left flank, leaving two narrow ribs above and below, and repeats this on the right flank.
He gives the left flank with the spine, the haunch with the tail and kidneys, and the last leg, so nine priests stand in line.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The first six priests hold the head, legs, forelegs, haunch, breast, flanks and innards in set positions.
Priests seven to nine carry the meal offering, griddle cakes and wine, then recite the Shema in the Chamber of Hewn Stone.
A baraita supports the binding of the lamb with a comparison to the binding of Isaac.
The mishna teaches that the lamb is not tied by fastening all four of its legs together.
What is the reason the lamb is not tied this way?
Rav Huna and Rav Hisda differ: tying is degrading to sacred items, or it imitates the nations' practices.
What is the practical difference between these two reasons?
The difference shows when the lamb is tied with silk or with a gold thread, which imitates the nations but is not degrading.
The Gemara cites a Shekalim mishna that the Temple had thirteen tables, as support for the marble tables.
Two more tables stood west of the ramp, one of marble for the limbs and one of silver for the service vessels.
Two tables inside the Entrance Hall, one of silver for fresh shewbread and one of gold for old shewbread.
The old shewbread is never moved from gold to silver, since one does not demote in matters of sanctity.
Since the Temple is a place of wealth, why were any tables made of marble rather than all silver or gold?
Gold and silver heat in the sun and spoil the limbs, so marble is used because metal scalds.
The morning daily offering is slaughtered at the northwest corner of the altar, on the second ring.
From where are these matters derived?
Rav Hisda cites the verse about the two daily lambs, meaning the lamb is slaughtered opposite the daylight.
A baraita teaches the same principle from the phrase two by day.
Does this mean opposite the light of day, or only that two lambs are offered each day?
The verse about one lamb in the morning and one in the afternoon states the daily obligation explicitly.
Therefore the phrase two by day means the lamb is slaughtered opposite the daylight.
How so, how is this principle applied to the morning and afternoon offerings?
Morning offering at the northwest corner's second ring, afternoon at the northeast, each opposite the sun.
Alexander of Macedon asked the Elders of the Negev about ten matters, starting with the position of the sun.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Alexander asks whether the distance from heaven to earth is greater than the distance from east to west.
The Elders reply that the distance from east to west is greater.
Evidence: the sun can be looked at in the east and west but not in mid-sky, so mid-sky is nearer.
The Sages hold that both distances are equal.
Psalm 103 compares God's kindness and removal of sins to the height of heaven and the distance from east to west.
If one distance were greater, the verse would have written only that one, so both must be equal.
Why, then, does no one look at the sun in mid-sky?
Because the sun there is exposed with nothing covering it, while in east or west it is partly screened.
Alexander asks whether the heavens or the earth were created first.
The Elders say the heavens were created first.
Genesis 1:1 says God created the heaven and the earth, which supports the heavens being first.
Alexander asks whether light or darkness was created first.
The Elders say the matter has no solution, as the verses do not indicate an answer.
The Gemara asks why they did not say darkness was created first.
Genesis 1:2 describes darkness before God said let there be light, supporting darkness first.
The Elders avoided answering so Alexander would not ask about forbidden matters of Creation.
If so, why did they answer the question about heaven but not the one about darkness?
At first they took his question as incidental; once he repeated the question, they withheld an answer.
Alexander asks who is truly worthy of being called wise.
The wise person is one who sees and anticipates the consequences of his behavior.
Alexander asks who is truly worthy of being called mighty.
The mighty person is one who masters his own desire.
Alexander asks who is truly worthy of being called wealthy.
The wealthy person is one who is content with his own portion.
Alexander asks what a man must do to ensure that he will live.
He must figuratively kill himself by living moderately.
Alexander asks what a man must do to ensure that he will die.
He must keep himself alive by leading an extravagant and indulgent life.
Alexander asks what a man must do to be accepted by people.
They say he must hate the king and the authorities and avoid those in power.
Alexander rejects their answer; one must love the king and authorities and use connections to benefit people.
Alexander asks whether it is better to live at sea or on dry land.
They say dry land is better, since seafarers' minds stay unsettled until they reach land.
Alexander asks who among them is wiser than the others.
They say all are equal in wisdom, since they solve every question he poses together.
Alexander asks what the substance of their stance against him is.
They reply that his dominance is inconsequential, since even the Satan sometimes wins over people.
Alexander declares that he will execute them by the edict of kings for their insolence.
They reply that the authority belongs to the king, but a king should not be made to lie.
Alexander dresses them in purple garments and places golden chains upon their necks.
Alexander says he wants to wage war in Africa and asks for their advice.
They say he cannot go, since the Mountains of Darkness block the passes.
Alexander says he cannot refrain from going and asks how to cross the Mountains of Darkness.
Bring Libyan donkeys that walk in darkness and coils of rope to mark the path back.
Alexander follows this advice and comes to a town whose entire population is women.
The women warn that fighting them would bring shame, since people would say a king was killed by women.
Alexander asks for bread, and they bring him bread of gold served on a golden table.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Alexander asks the women whether people eat bread made of gold.
The women reply that he came for wealth, not bread, since he had bread at home.
Alexander's inscription on the town gate says he learned sense from women in Africa.
Eating bread by a spring, Alexander smells a fragrance and concludes the spring flows from the Garden of Eden.
Some say he washed his face in the spring; others say he followed it up to the Garden of Eden.
Alexander calls out at the Garden's gate, asking for it to be opened for him.
The Garden's sentry cites Psalm 118 that only the righteous may enter the Lord's gate.
Alexander argues he is a king and asks for something from inside; they give him one eyeball.
He weighs all his gold and silver against the eyeball, yet it outweighs them all.
Alexander asks the Sages what this is and why the eyeball outweighs everything.
It is the eye of a mortal, which is never satisfied.
Alexander asks from where they know this is the reason.
Covering the eye with a little dirt immediately balances the scale.
Proverbs 27:20 says the eyes of man are never satisfied, supporting the Sages' explanation.
The school of Eliyahu taught that Gehenna is above the heavens, or beyond the Mountains of Darkness.
R. Hiyya taught that the Divine Presence faces anyone who studies Torah at night.
Lamentations 2:19 is cited to support the Divine Presence facing one who studies at night.
R. Elazar ben Azarya taught that Torah scholars increase peace in the world.
Isaiah 54:13 is cited to support that scholars build and increase peace.
Mishna 5:1: after laying the limbs, the priests recite Shema with a single blessing and three people's blessings.
Mishna 5:2: only new incense priests join the incense lottery, and those who won the ramp-limbs lottery take them up.
R. Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that the priest who carries limbs up the ramp is the one who places them on the altar.
Mishna 5:3: priests who lost the lottery are undressed by attendants, and the vestments are stored by type in compartments.
Mishna 5:4: the priest who won the incense lottery takes the spoon, which holds three kav.

ranges.en: The incense vessel was filled to overflow, with a cover and cloth to keep its fragrance in.
Mishna 5:5: the priest carries silver and gold coal pans from the outer altar and spills about one kav of coals.
On Shabbat a large pesakhter is overturned over coals, and it serves three purposes, including removing ashes from the altar.
Mishna 5:6: a priest throws the shovel between the Entrance Hall and the altar, so its sound drowns out speech in Jerusalem.
The shovel's sound serves three purposes: it summons priests and Levites to their service and sets impure priests apart.
Mishna 6:1: the priests begin ascending the Entrance Hall stairs, and the ash-removers clear the Sanctuary vessels.
The Candelabrum priest checks the lamps, leaves one burning for the afternoon, and takes the jug of ashes out.
Mishna 6:2: the priest spreads the coals from the coal pan evenly on the inner altar, then leaves.
Mishna 6:3: the incense priest gives the spoon's incense to an assistant and is taught to scatter it carefully.
The incense is burned only after the appointed priest tells him to, addressing the High Priest with respect.
No one may stand between the Entrance Hall and the outer altar during incense, derived from Leviticus 16:17.
The chapter closes and the next mishna begins, on ascending the stairs of the Entrance Hall.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna 7:1: the High Priest enters the Sanctuary held by three priests, and the appointed priest lifts the curtain for his exit.
Mishna 7:2: five priests stand on the stairs holding the five vessels used in the morning service.
The priests bless the people with one blessing in the Temple, and the name of God is pronounced as written.
Outside the Temple priests lift their hands to their shoulders, but in the Temple they raise them above their heads.
R. Yehuda holds that even the High Priest raises his hands above the frontplate when blessing the people.
Leviticus 9:22 says Aaron lifted his hands and blessed the people, supporting R. Yehuda's view.
Mishna 7:3: the High Priest burns the limbs at the altar, the deputy supports him, and the limbs are handed to him.
The High Priest circles the altar starting from the southeast corner and then pours the wine libation at the southwest.
The deputy waves the cloths as signal, and two priests sound the trumpet blasts to alert the Levites.
The Levites sing the psalm in three sections with a tekia and prostration after each; a closing prayer for rebuilding follows.
Mishna 7:4: the psalm the Levites sing on each day of the week, from Psalm 24 on Sunday to Psalm 92 on Shabbat.
The chapter closes with the case of the High Priest, and the tractate of Tamid concludes.
